title: Before you go
hook: anyone is welcome; cover your head, take off your shoes, bring no tobacco or alcohol

segments.voice: Yesterday, your Nitnem, for now. Your line was one bani, daily. Did you say or play the one you chose this morning? Now we step out of the house, to a new stretch: the gurdwara. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

Walking into a place of worship that isn't yours can feel like walking into a stranger's kitchen. Where do I stand? What do I touch? What if I do something wrong and everybody notices? Plenty of people drive past a gurdwara for years, curious, and never go in, because nobody told them the rules. So before the next week of visiting, here's the simple part: what to know before you go. And the first thing to know is the most important. You're allowed in.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KITCHEN.` → `WHAT IF I GET IT WRONG?` → `YOU'RE ALLOWED IN.`

segments.voice: Gurdwara means the door of the Guru, or the Guru's gateway. It's the Sikh place of worship, and its doors are open to everyone: Sikhs, people of any other faith, people of none. That openness is written into Sikh history. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, was built with entrances on all four sides, and Sikhs have long read that as a sign that people from every direction and every background are welcome. It's also built lower than the ground around it, so you step down to enter. So what do you actually do? Just a few things, all about respect for the Guru Granth Sahib, which is present in the main hall. Cover your head. Men, women and children all do this. A scarf, a bandana, anything that covers the hair. Most gurdwaras keep a basket of head coverings by the door if you forget. Take off your shoes. There's usually a shoe rack or a room for them, and often a place to wash your hands, and sometimes your feet. Bring no tobacco, alcohol or drugs, not even in a pocket. Sikhs don't use them, and they don't come into the gurdwara. Dress modestly, and expect to sit on the floor. That's it. Nobody will ask what you believe. Nobody will ask you to join anything. If you're unsure what to do next, someone will almost always show you, often with a smile and a plate of food. Sikhs are proud of their hospitality, and the gurdwara is where it lives.
screen: `GURDWARA — THE GURU'S DOOR.` · `FOUR DOORS, EVERY DIRECTION.` · `HEAD COVERED, SHOES OFF.` · `NO TOBACCO, NO ALCOHOL.` · then, large: `EVERYONE IS WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Find your nearest gurdwara. If you have a map app, search for gurdwara now and see how far the closest one is. You might be surprised. There are gurdwaras in small towns and big cities on every continent. If you'd rather not look now, just picture arriving at one: slipping off your shoes, tying a scarf over your hair, washing your hands, stepping inside. Notice what you feel: curiosity, nerves, both. The bell holds the time.
Before you go. The gurdwara is open to everyone: cover your head, take off your shoes, bring no tobacco or alcohol, and you're welcome.
Your line: everyone is welcome. Today, find one place where you could make someone else feel welcome, and do it the gurdwara's way, with a smile and something to eat. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Visitors of any faith are welcome in a gurdwara; they cover their heads, remove their shoes, wash their hands, bring no tobacco or alcohol, and sit on the floor in the main hall.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gurdwara, the door or gateway of the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh temple, for Sikhs.
what it means: the Guru's door, open to anyone who covers their head, takes off their shoes and leaves tobacco and alcohol outside.
what a scholar hears: the Harmandir Sahib's four entrances, and its floor set below the ground around it, are read as openness and humility.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Akal Takht (conduct in the gurdwara; prohibition of tobacco)
Sikh tradition: the four entrances of the Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar

notes: The four entrances of the Harmandir Sahib as a sign of welcome to all four directions and castes: a widely told reading. Confirm phrasing.
Harmandir Sahib set lower than the surrounding ground (stepping down to enter) as a sign of humility: common explanation. Confirm.
Some gurdwaras also ask visitors to wash feet; described as 'sometimes'. Confirm.
